candidates.attacker_control: The type-id string in the JSON payload is fully attacker-controlled: either the synthetic `@class` property created by `enableDefaultTypingAsProperty` / `@JsonTypeInfo(As.PROPERTY)`, or the leading string element of the wrapper array used by the default `As.WRAPPER_ARRAY` mode. No allowlist, subtype-confinement (only `isTypeOrSubTypeOf` for generic ids containing '<', line 58), or caller-supplied package restriction applies beyond the ten exact names at BeanDeserializerFactory.java:53-63.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Default typing is disabled by default, so exposure requires explicit configuration or Id.CLASS annotations. `checkIllegalTypes` does execute for the ordinary bean path (createBeanDeserializer:173), and the well-known CVE-2017-7525 gadgets (InvokerTransformer, InstantiateTransformer, ConvertedClosure, MethodClosure, ObjectFactory, TemplatesImpl x2, JdbcRowSetImpl) are blocked. No gadget library is declared in this pom.xml, so in-repo impact is conditional on the host application's classpath. The generic-id branch does enforce subtype relation (ClassNameIdResolver:52-63). I found no evidence that any of the ten 2.8.9-era entries is missing or mutated. The claim that specific unblocked classes are exploitable gadgets is external/domain knowledge and is not verifiable from this snapshot.
candidates.impact: When a suitable non-blocked gadget class is on the classpath, a remote, unauthenticated JSON payload can drive that class's deserialization side effects, potentially reaching code execution (e.g., JNDI lookups, remote bean-definition loading) or SSRF/file access depending on the gadget; at minimum the incomplete list fails its stated purpose and permits instantiation of arbitrary classes by name.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The application enables default typing (ObjectMapper.java:1392/1402/1418/1442) or annotates a polymorphic property/base type with `@JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.CLASS)`; 2) attacker can submit JSON to a readValue path reaching that type; 3) a class usable as a deserialization gadget whose fully-qualified name is not one of the ten blocked names is present on the application classpath (e.g., Spring context/AOP classes, JDK logging/RMI classes known to have been added to later upstream denylists). Default typing is opt-in, so non-configured applications are not exposed by this path.
candidates.root_cause: Class-name-driven polymorphic deserialization (`enableDefaultTyping*`, `@JsonTypeInfo(use=Id.CLASS)`) is gated only by an exact-match denylist of ten class names in BeanDeserializerFactory. `checkIllegalTypes()` (lines 896-908) rejects a type only if `_cfgIllegalClassNames.contains(fullName)`; every other class name is loaded via `Class.forName(name, true, TCCL)` and bound as a bean, so any gadget class not present in this fixed list can still be instantiated and populated with attacker-chosen properties.
candidates.title: Incomplete exact-name denylist for default-typing/polymorphic deserialization allows non-blocked gadget classes to be loaded and bound (deserialization RCE)
candidates.trace: ObjectMapper.readValue -> deserializer for declared type -> TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer (line 150) -> ClassNameIdResolver.typeFromId/_typeFromId (line 67 `tf.findClass(id)`, line 81 constructSpecializedType) -> TypeFactory.findClass -> Class.forName(name, true, contextClassLoader) (TypeFactory.java:288/294) -> DeserializationContext.findContextualValueDeserializer:443 -> DeserializerCache._createAndCache2:244 -> BeanDeserializerFactory.createBeanDeserializer:128 -> checkIllegalTypes:173/896-908 (exact-name contains check only) -> buildBeanDeserializer -> reflective creator/setter/field binding of attacker-chosen property values, invoking gadget side effects.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution or exploit reproduction was performed and none is provided. Specific gadget chains for the named non-blocked classes were not verified in this repository (they reside in third-party libraries absent here). The exact fix commit/issue numbers for this version line were inferred from source state and version metadata, not from repository history. Whether the grading ground truth targets CVE-2017-15095, CVE-2017-17485, or a later blacklist extension cannot be determined from source alone; all share this code location and root cause.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (incomplete blocklist / gadget-class deserialization)

coverage_summary: Scope: 407 visible repository files (400 main-source Java files, pom/README/travis/attic files). Relation index: 400 parsed files (1 omitted), 0 parse errors, 8,457 symbols, 20,416 edges, but semantic resolution, control flow, and data flow are explicitly not implemented and 7,972 calls are unresolved, so all relation data was used only for navigation and verified in source text. I inspected the polymorphic deserialization chain end-to-end (ObjectMapper default-typing builders, TypeDeserializerBase, ClassNameIdResolver, TypeFactory/ClassUtil class loading, DeserializerCache, BeanDeserializerFactory denylist and createBeanDeserializer), the access-override/reflection machinery, MapperFeature defaults, XML/DOM deserializers, DataFormatReaders lookahead, and sampled sibling implementations (AsArray/AsWrapper type deserializers, SettableAnyProperty). No src/test directory is present, so no repository tests corroborate behavior. Files outside these paths (e.g., most serializer/node/introspection code) were only sampled or listed, not read line-by-line.
limitations: No execution, tests, or exploit payloads were run; every statement about behavior is source-derived, and exploitability is conditional on host classpath/configuration.

The relation index provides only syntactic name/containment/call candidates with no data-flow or reachability proof; unresolved calls (7,972) mean some paths may be missing from the index and I did not claim coverage of index-absent code.
One source file is omitted from the index/build metrics and some binary-like content is skipped by the tooling; it was not inspected.

The denylist's completeness can only be assessed against external knowledge of published gadget classes; that gadget behavior is not verifiable within this snapshot and no gadget library is declared in the project pom.

The precise upstream fix (issue/CVE) matching this snapshot could not be established from repository contents alone; version metadata (2.8.10-SNAPSHOT) and code-annotation dates were used as circumstantial evidence only.
No git history, patch, or ground-truth material was consulted or available, so I could not diff this snapshot against the released 2.8.10 artifact.

rejected_leads.lead: Abstract-type materialization path in BeanDeserializerFactory.createBeanDeserializer (lines 150-159) builds the materialized concrete type without calling checkIllegalTypes.
rejected_leads.reason: The materialized class comes from an application-registered AbstractTypeResolver, not attacker input; no source evidence that an attacker can influence the resolver mapping. Unconfirmed and materially weaker than the denylist gap.
The builder class is selected by application annotations (@JsonDeserialize(builder=...)), not by the JSON payload, so it is not an attacker-controlled control point.

rejected_leads.lead: Recursive/deep-nesting stack exhaustion in UntypedObjectDeserializer/TokenBuffer/JsonNode for very deep payloads.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible general resource-exhaustion hardening gap, but no specific broken check or trigger was verified in source, and it is a different root cause from the selected candidate; excluded to respect the one-candidate cap.

Reflective access is intended behavior gated by MapperFeature.CAN_OVERRIDE_ACCESS_MODIFIERS (default true, MapperFeature.java:169) and OVERRIDE_PUBLIC_ACCESS_MODIFIERS; defaults match upstream and this is an application-level privilege decision, not an attacker-controlled bypass.
Already hardened: setExpandEntityReferences(false) and XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING are set (DOMDeserializer.java:31-41); no missing check found.
className values are fixed private constants (e.g., JSR-275/Joda implementations), not attacker-derived; not a controllable sink.

summary: Reviewed jackson-databind 2.8.10-SNAPSHOT (407 visible files; 400 Java files parsed by the relation index, 1 file omitted, 0 parse errors). The strongest source-evidenced security issue is the incomplete exact-name denylist that is the sole guard for class-name-based polymorphic deserialization: `BeanDeserializerFactory.DEFAULT_NO_DESER_CLASS_NAMES` contains only 10 names, `checkIllegalTypes()` does a single exact `contains()` test, and every other attacker-supplied type id is loaded with `Class.forName` and bound as a bean. Known deserialization gadget classes absent from this list (e.g., Spring context/AOP classes, `java.util.logging.FileHandler`, `java.rmi.server.UnicastRemoteObject`) therefore remain deserializable when default typing is enabled, giving a gadget-mediated RCE/SSRF class of impact. This is a documented weakness of this version line, and the 2.8.10-SNAPSHOT code state (blacklist with #1680 entry but no later entries; newest annotation 17-Aug-2017) is consistent with being just before an upstream blacklist-extension fix. I found no evidence of a synthetic logic mutation elsewhere in the sampled high-risk paths (type resolution, class loading, access override, XML parsing, feature defaults).
